name: Griffin
pages: I met Griffin at a cuddle convention. The premise, supposedly, is that cuddling can be a platonic activity — "touch without meaning." Well. I am here to report that a cuddle convention, put on by a lot of shitty people as a sad excuse for not having a valentine on Valentine's Day, is not the place where this is likely to take place. It was Valentine's Day, and Alpha and I, having just met and "moved in" together, had decided we weren't staying home; hypothetically, we both wanted to find love. On the bus we made fun of a woman who got on and off with us, then realized she was going exactly where we were going. Worse: when we arrived at political-correctness headquarters, Alpha joked to a woman standing outside that the whole consent conversation was a load of bullshit that didn't need half an hour — and then we walked in, and that woman was standing at the front of the room, speaking. Behind her, a chalkboard listed polite ways to say no. First we practiced rescinding consent. She tried to make it fun by inventing cuddle positions — the alligator, where one person's legs open like an alligator's mouth — but the fun was mostly ruined by Alpha sweating nervously at the back. Then we walked the one block to the actual cuddle room, the second layer of hell, where we discussed, with the people we were about to cuddle, what saying no felt like. Lucky me: my partner was one of the event's organizers. We took turns asking to touch parts of each other's bodies. I asked if I could touch her hair, and she said, "no, because I don't think you would be comfortable with that" — then raised her hand and announced to the whole group that she'd said no because she didn't really think I wanted to touch her hair. Pointing at me. The creepy one, who'd asked for what they could not have.

Then we got into groups and pretended to be animals — crawling like hippos, cuddling like giraffes. Most people chose to be cats or dogs, which I supposed was the point: the platonic cuddle made flesh. I was a sloth. I did not move at all. I waited for the torture to be over. In the final round of cuddling, I inadvertently found the one attractive male in this sea of potential cuddlers, and perhaps he'd done the same, because we gravitated slowly toward each other — a tall boy with a blonde ponytail — along with a woman who told us she was asexual but still liked human contact. Pillow talk was hopping in our little cuddle threesome, what with him trying to hit on me without hitting on her: we discussed how much we enjoyed that one could cuddle platonically, nothing sexual about it at all, as his hand snaked its way slowly toward my butt and I moved it gently away. After that came the Valentine's dance, preceded by a barbaric form of slam poetry in which the audience stands up on their chairs to vote for the poem they liked best — a great idea, unless your poem did not do well and you stared out at a crowd of the seated. I never did like slam poetry, so I stayed in my seat. In the spirit of the convention, we held hands the whole way to the dance — myself, the tall blonde boy, a girl with straight hair, and Alpha. A little hard to pass a four-person cuddle monster on the sidewalk, but, as I always say, "cuddling trumps passerby traffic." At the dance, Griffin ignored me, touching and flirting with the girl to his left — a petite brunette in glasses and a bright red dress. All evening you could watch his mind turning, working the problem of how to get the two of us into bed with him together. I wasn't necessarily opposed — not because I was interested in her, but it seemed like an interesting experience to navigate, figuring out what my role would be. She seemed less interested, and eventually left him for a boy who appeared near the end of the evening in a motorcycle helmet, and who was, ostensibly, already her partner.

For the final round, Griffin and I went upstairs and sat next to each other drinking a cider he'd bought, and he made a speech about how much power he had, about his ability to control people, and about how interested I was in having sex with him — at the end of which he asked me how much I wanted to. I had been thinking no such thing, and told him so, and he backtracked, seeming embarrassed. He also told me he liked the barbarian lifestyle: that in some situations he might act barbaric, or barbarous, if the situation fit — circumstantially only, he insisted; normally he was civilized. Then he laid out his plan to bed me and the other girl together, and, for the sake of being unpredictable, I agreed — but first I wandered off to take a call from my brother, who reported that he'd seen two salamanders making love in an aquarium that day. God's Valentine's Day gift to the world. Talking to my brother, my voice changed into the voice of someone familiar, someone with things in common, and I think it put my date off. Downstairs, Griffin asked her whether she wanted to do this. She said no. Then we both started dancing with other people. Whatever energy there had been between us had clearly dissipated, but the plan was the plan, so we left together and got on a bus toward his house. At his street I told him I wanted to go home, and he asked if it was because I was afraid he would force me to do something I wasn't comfortable with. I said that was the case. He assured me he would do no such thing, so I agreed, apprehensively. At his house we cuddled on the couch, discussing once more the advantages of cuddling outside a romantic or sexual context. He carried me to his room; I insisted I no longer wanted to have sex with him. We got naked and did not do anything sexual. In the morning I looked at his extensive Lego collection and he made me eggs, then played a video game while I talked on the phone to my friend Alessio. A few months later I ran into him at a party, but I was with another boy, and I didn't want to talk to him.

name: David
pages: David's photos were abnormal, emphasizing his creamy complexion. He seemed very young for a man — he was in fact two years younger than me — but after some banter about cats and dreams, we agreed to meet at an all-night coffee house I rarely visited during the day. When I arrived he had already ordered, and stood as far from the counter as humanly possible, so as not to be confused for the one paying. I ordered a chai tea. We sat at a round table and he talked about studying computer science, and I remember thinking, for some reason, that this could be the one. Then I got a bit annoyed, because he wasn't making conversation — I was talking fast and asking questions, and he was sitting far back in his chair, being quiet. I told him I shouldn't finish my chai or I'd get even more hyper. He said I should drink the rest and see how hyper I could get — which didn't match the impression I'd been getting, so I gave him a few points, and let him finish it instead. At the bus stop I hugged the pole of the bus sign and swung around it and said this was the same as paying the fare, while he stood upright, checking his phone, nervous the bus wouldn't come on time. He refused to tell me his height in anything but centimeters — something about the system being flawed — and took this strange hill much further than I would have guessed. I still don't know how tall he is. At his house, he told me his roommate had never once brought a date over, so all this was very surprising to him. They had beef: both vegetarian, but she'd recently gone vegan and was now shaming him for keeping butter in the fridge. I couldn't imagine how two such polite people had come to harbor such total and complete resentment. Then we made pasta, and he instructed me to grate a giant block of cheddar, and when I switched to a second, larger grater that worked better, he became very pissy that I'd used two cheese graters — two graters to clean, instead of one. I was starting to see how he might be having difficulty getting along with his roommate.

His roommate came home peppy, with her date; they cuddled on the couch with beers and invited us to watch Lost in Translation. Next to the couch was a seat salvaged from a car, which still had the lever to make it lean back. David sat in the car chair, said nothing further, and refused the beer they offered — I accepted mine — and when they suggested a second movie, he said that they could, but that he didn't want to, and that he could take me home if I wanted. In the garage he had a motorcycle. It was at that moment I realized I had to pee — which wouldn't do for my first time on a motorcycle. He'd forgotten our helmets inside, and, panicked, I squatted in his shed, hoping to somehow finish before he came back, but the thought of him reappearing at any moment made me pee-shy. He came out, handed me a helmet, and we rode home, and it was exhilarating. Inside, we decided to play chess and take it outside; the sheds in the backyard wouldn't open, and eventually we abandoned the game and stood awkwardly in the kitchen, saying goodbye without touching. The next time, he picked me up from my house and we drank beer at the park, then went back to his and played Nooki and fell asleep holding hands, a cat between us. I dreamt there was another girl in our bed — Molly, maybe — who looked like his cat. He went to school in the morning, and when he got back we had tea in the kitchen, went to Los Gorditos and shared a quesadilla, then got the ladder so he could climb onto his roof, where he cut part of the tree down. Afterwards we watched the dream movie with his roommate, and then he took me to 51 Licks, and then he drove me home.

name: Jake
dek: A hot babe on my lap.
pages: Through the window of the Southeast Grind I saw the most attractive person I had ever encountered, outside, having a cigarette. I figured he was passing through, and that I would never talk to him or anything. Instead he came and sat three seats away at the counter, drawing in a sketchbook. One by one, the people between us left. I sprawled crazily across all three empty seats, stomach on the middle one, and asked if I could see what he was drawing. He showed me. It wasn't anything particularly impressive — a washed-out nature scene, in watercolor — and immediately I was turned off. But I was already there, sprawled across three seats. He asked if I wanted to play chess. Of course. He got the board from the games closet and set it up in an interested silence — he never asked whether I knew how to play, or whether I was any good, which flattered me. But a few moves in I got bored, and started to act out. Rather than moving my pawn two spaces, I moved it three. He didn't say anything. He took his turn. I took mine. I moved a knight into a cluster of his pieces. I moved his pieces. I moved two of my own at once. I returned dead pieces to the board. Finally I killed my king with my own queen and moved it off the board, so that no one could win — and we continued anyway, until he had about ten pieces left and I had one white pawn darting around all of them, whether it was my turn or not. "You win," I said. He agreed, and set up the board again. I won the second game too. Through all of it he remained stony-faced and unperturbed, following the rules without comment.

Outside, I leaned on him, his dark sweatshirt against mine, the cigarette in his hand. He sat down and had me sit on his lap. A friend of his came over and asked how he was. "Can't complain," Jake said. "I got a hot babe on my lap and a hot cigarette on my lips." He pulled at the lining of my dress — "Is this a… scarf?" — and leaned forward to kiss my mouth, but I turned my head the other way, so that we would not be intimate. Then I turned around and put my arms around his neck and my legs around his stomach. "You're a little koala, aren't you?" he said, in something like disbelief. He was an artist, he said; he came to the Grind because it was the only place open all night, and he liked to work on his art there. And then we were walking to his art studio downtown, a long walk, into streets I'd seldom explored, him carrying my Thomas the Tank Engine backpack in his hand like a clutch. "Is there anything you want to know about me?" he asked, finally, into the silence. We passed a garbage-disposal building. "I used to work there," he said. At the studio he made noodles in a silver cylinder with a pouring spout, in what I could not imagine were clean pans, and offered me the aux cord. I put on Gucci Mane. "You like Gucci Mane?" he asked, surprised. He offered me noodles; I shook my head no; and just as he was almost done eating, I said, "actually, can I have some?" As soon as he'd finished, he said, "Hey — do you wanna go to my loft?" I didn't answer. He was already climbing the ladder. It was dark up there, and we looked at each other, and it just happened that we started kissing, and he stopped to replace the wooden board that was the door to the ladder. "You're the first girl I've brought here," he said, with a goofy grin.

In the morning he said he had to get up in a little bit, and I sat up and started collecting my phone and clothes, and he put his hand around my waist and pulled me backwards, so that I was curled up in front of him. "We can sleep a bit more." The room was warm and soaked in sun, and I enjoyed being held in place. When we finally got up, a whiff of insanity came over me, an extreme airiness; I felt better watching him lace his combat boots back onto his feet, pulling each lace tight. I imagined they were steel-toed. He asked if I wanted to take a shower and I said "yeah!" — and then, when I tried to come into the shower with him, he explained, as though I were a child, that some experiences were personal, and that he liked to shower by himself. Afterwards, through the bathroom door, I listened to Jake and a voice I didn't recognize invent, together, a wooden butt plug. I'll spare you their reasoning. He walked me to the nearest street corner. "So, did you want my number?" I went through the motions of putting him in my phone, first name only, since I didn't know his last and didn't care to ask. He seemed to notice, and told me he rarely gives girls his number. I hugged him around the middle and said "bye." Then I walked, rather purposefully, away — into a part of downtown Portland I'd never been to. I called my friend Adam, and then Charlie, and then Alessio, and sat alone at a four-person table in a greasy Chinese place, eating a few bites of fried beige noodles — too salty, and the noodles too fried. Adam was high and bored and not interested in my experience. Charlie was mean to me for reasons I couldn't locate. And then a text arrived from Alessio, saying that our somewhat romantic friendship made him feel he was cheating on his girlfriend, and that he could no longer be friends with me. My stomach dropped. I started walking slowly in the direction of home, and somewhere along the side of the highway I stopped being upset and was just sad, which is different. I found a bus stop I knew, and it was so easy to get home — all I had to do was wait for the bus to get there. I spent a quiet night at home.

name: Blake
dek: Points for pretending I didn't speak Spanish.
pages: My date with Blake was set up to take place in the middle of a forest. He gave me intentionally obscure directions to meet him on a fallen tree at a trail in downtown Portland — exactly the quirky premise I'd been hoping for, which is, of course, why I agreed. I didn't let myself set an alarm, even though I was to meet him at ten in the morning, and I had my roommate plan my route on his computer, since Google Maps wasn't working on my phone. On the bus, sun slanting through the windows, I got wrapped up in wondering what all the other passengers might be doing on this strange day — people with lives, I supposed, while I tried to imagine explaining the purpose of my own trip. It reminded me of being excused from school with a doctor's note, allowed for once to lounge on the sunny couches in my parents' bedroom while the sun hit them from an unfamiliar angle — reality shifted a fraction of an inch to one side. I stared at the spot on the map that was supposed to be my hiking trail, saw only concrete out the window, and decided I must be crazy to imagine that beyond all these streets I would find myself in an all-consuming wilderness. So I stayed seated while the bus carried me to the completely wrong end of town. When I realized my mistake, I began to panic — waves of caution I hadn't felt since I nervously awaited a teacher's realization that I had not, as instructed, written six pages. It was a wake-up call: why were there exactly zero moments of this kind of terror in my daily life? I couldn't remember the last time I'd felt this alive, and though it wasn't pleasant, I resolved to do more things — the vaguest of plans. I texted him that I was lost. He said he was enjoying what he was doing in his tree, and that it would still be there when I got there. A lot of points for him. I finally found the trail opening and proceeded up it as instructed, then checked the rest of the directions: past three fallen trees and across two wooden bridges, and I'd find him. I felt scared and discouraged — I hadn't come to even one of the markers. I went back. I texted him. I went forward. I sat down on the trail and, though my battery was low, listened to Blue by Animal Collective, to collect myself. I met two women and asked if they'd seen any wooden bridges, and they had — a little farther up — so with renewed determination I walked the way I'd been going all along, got confused again, and called him.

He agreed to meet me at the trail entrance, where I gulped from the water fountain with complete delight, like a deer at a watering hole, which is something I feel like almost all the time anyway. I had made him wait on his tree for two hours. He approached in a punk-rock t-shirt, hair long, a healthy height and weight, not particularly set on impressing me; the strangeness of our meeting place went unacknowledged by both of us, and we kept going. We went to get a burger. On the way, he told me all about his weed-trimming business — how good it was for him, how he didn't feel guilty about it — and I said nothing, because I was not remotely interested. I didn't let him pay for me. I knew by then that I didn't like him, and it wouldn't have been fair to accept free food without reciprocating. We played a game where we each wrote parts of stories on the little pads of paper from my purse, and I lied about not speaking Spanish to prove a point I was making. He asked, on a scale of one to ten, how the date was going for me; I declined to answer. It was about a seven for him, he said — I'd earned points for persevering on the hike, and for pretending I didn't speak Spanish to make a racist point. Then he told me he'd written his ex-girlfriend's senior thesis for her, because she was Asian and couldn't write English that well. We moved to a couch with a mirror, his arm around me, and we might have kissed. I said I was really tired and just wanted a nap, which was true; I'd gotten very little sleep the night before. Getting home, we boarded a bus that seemed to be going the wrong way, got off, discovered it hadn't been, and waited in the median to get back on. The bus was nice, actually: he was self-conscious about talking with so many people around, so we just sat, his arm around me, neither of us saying much. At my house I went in first and lay down on my bed. He came in and seemed uncomfortable — this wasn't what he'd been expecting. He wanted to cuddle. I said I really just wanted to nap, because I was by then a little disgusted by him, by how much he had talked. But his trying to convince me made me reconsider — it was an interesting thing, arguing that we should cuddle — until finally he asked if he was ever going to see me again. I said no. He said alright, fine. Eventually I got up and walked him to the bus stop I'd found on my GPS, and waved goodbye when he got on. That night I went to the Southeast Grind, and Jake was there, flirting with a blonde girl on the couch. They left together. He ignored me.

name: Louis
pages: Louis was so very cute in all of his pictures, and I couldn't believe he'd want to meet me. He said something about it being "Caturday" — the day for cats. When he arrived he was cute in person too, and very lovely, and casually claimed my roommate's giant yoga ball, bouncing, while I took the rolly chair. He'd started doing yoga recently, he told me, and he liked dancing. We went to Buffalo Exchange on Hawthorne, where he tried on leggings — though first we tried on hats together — and then, while he waited in the chair beside me, I applied for a job, filling out the application until someone came over and interviewed me on the spot. We had trouble finding the car, and it was starting to rain. We found a Mexican restaurant with almost a tiki theme to it, extravagant vegetation climbing to the ceiling, and I was confused about which cocktail to order, not being used to ordering cocktails, so we each chose something different and shared. He told me about his old relationship — five years, ended by small things going wrong — and then said he felt bad for talking so long. No, I said, it was interesting, keep going; so he told me about his next adventure, in which he would go pick weed leaves and then take ayahuasca. He drove me home so I could change my pants, and then we went to a dance club I'd never been to called Bossa Nova: a live band of three probably elderly gentlemen, disco lights in the floor, booths where people drank extravagant cocktails and maybe even smoked cigars. We found ourselves smack in the middle of the dance floor, where it was very hot, and though we were dancing together, he had yet to so much as grab my wrist. This went on for a long while as I contemplated what might be going on — this seemed an obvious time to invite physical contact — until I said fuck it, broke the rules, and leaned my hand casually on his hip. Then we got two more drinks each and started making out in one of the booths. He drove us back through the rain, and we made out in the car, and his fingers traveled southward, and he asked if I wanted to go inside the house. Inside, we almost went further, but he asked me if I wanted to, and I said no, so we didn't. He rolled over and slept completely separate from me, falling asleep quickly while I watched his slow breathing. He left fairly early the next morning.

name: Patrick
dek: Like a tiger, or a man proving a point.
pages: I meet Patrick on the street; he has just come from the 7-Eleven with a beer. His carefully constructed hipster outfit incorporates a lumberjack-like plaid flannel and large horn-rimmed frames, and atop his head sits a messy bun from his silky mane of light ginger strands. I am wearing my customary black tight dress with my black skeleton long-sleeve over it and my black Harley-Davidson boots — I've worn all of it for the past week and a half, because none of my other clothes are clean. On our way we pass Michael, seated at a table in front of an open laptop, wearing his signature gray cardigan and what seems to be his only t-shirt, whose tiny holes make it possible to see part of his bare chest shining translucent in the moonlight. He joins us for more beer. I buy a very dark porter in a handsome glass bottle — not a single beer but a 40, much too much for me to drink by myself, but I am feeling ambitious. Outside, I find the two of them amiably comparing notes on what they hate about America, gesturing rapidly, the word capitalism interjected every few seconds. Both want to move as soon as possible, maybe to China or India, where things are cheaper and more community-oriented and there isn't so much capitalism. I can't quite bring myself to join, and stare instead at the bumps in the paved lot, and at the white poles holding up the gas-station canopy, and at the dark night behind it all. The more the merrier, you might think — but no: my friend and my date claim each other's attention entirely, leaving none for yours truly. Then an overweight stranger pulls up in a beat-up van and, while his car fills with gas, approaches me — only me — to ask if I have a cigarette. I note his gauges, a nose piercing, khaki shorts. I am, frankly, pleased to finally have a companion of my own. Patrick says he'll give him one for fifty cents. The stranger digs fifty cents from his pocket. Then, cigarette acquired, he goes back to ignoring my two companions, looks straight at me, and asks, quite aggressively, who these boys are. I answer frankly: I'm on a date with one; the other is my friend. He asks — glancing at Patrick only long enough to gesture at him — whether I feel safe with my date.

"Look, you can't just, like, insult my date like that or whatever, ok. He's, like, a person and all." I'm hoping this impromptu confrontation might at least have the effect that no one utters the word capitalism for the rest of the night. Michael says nothing and does nothing, a shit-eating grin plastered across his face. Patrick stalks closer and closer to the stranger, until he is centimeters from his head, staring with his magnificent dark eyes. Like a tiger. Or like a man trying to prove a point. "If we were to fight — just saying — you'd be dead. On the ground in one second." Then Patrick wraps his arm lightly around the stranger's back: "You guys look gay. Oh look, I think they're gay — don't you think they might be, like, maybe just a little bit gay, or something? No? I think they might be." Michael and I stare at each other across the circle, a hint of mirth on our lips and confusion in our eyes, as our two new friends square up to fight each other over nothing. Finally I say to the stranger, "do you, like, really wanna hit something, or what? Cause, you can just hit me." He doesn't believe me at first. "It'll be fine, I think. No, seriously." We go back and forth until he delivers a light slap to the side of my face — not so light as I was expecting. After that, I can think of nothing to do but leave, and so Patrick and I make our way home, while the stranger presumably returns to his van, and Michael, from the corner of my eye, seats himself at a nearby picnic table. Tension successfully diffused. To what end, exactly, I can't be sure. At home, I fulfill my promise of letting him sleep in my bed — except he isn't ready to sleep. I simply want to; Patrick lies awake beside me, pleading that I haven't gotten a chance to know him, that I've prejudged him, that I've made a mistake. In the morning he smokes out of a pipe he brought and leaves the ashes on our communal table, where my roommate — this is a substance-free household — sees them before I can. He texts me later, thanking me for the show. I can only suppose how his account might differ from mine. Still, I think he would be the main character, since I can't think of anything out of the ordinary that I said or did.

name: Trevor
dek: He smashed a beer bottle on his head.
pages: Trevor called before the date with a question: did I have any ex-boyfriends who might be out to get him? Someone had just phoned and threatened him not to go out with his girl. I told him I wasn't sure who it could be, but assumed it wasn't related to me. He didn't sound convinced. He sounded a little angry — at me, somehow, already. He showed up twenty minutes later anyway and ordered a coffee with four shots. He was very cute but not very big, a bit like Drake from Drake and Josh, in skinny jeans and a black t-shirt. We drove to The Florida Room and took the outdoor patio, where he bought us tequila shots and we read our poetry to each other. He knew the bartender — the bartender who always poured him extra-full shots — which is how I came to be very drunk, drifting over to other people's tables to talk with them for a while and then inform them they were boring, until Trevor escorted me out. His house was two blocks away; he lived on the top level, and I made a lot of noise in the bathroom. On the stairs up to his attic room, the light caught something on his face: scratches. I asked about them — though I only know that because he told me the next day; by then the night had gaps in it. His ex-girlfriend had done something to upset him, he said, so he'd smashed a beer bottle over his own head, to try to kill himself. It seemed like a strange story to tell on a first date, but he offered it easily, like it was nothing. In the morning he handed me the remote and said I could put on any movie I wanted, so I put on Fear and Loathing in Las Vegas. The sun came in sweet and yellow, and the colors were so pastel and opaque that I decided it was my favorite movie; as it went on, I liked it less, and realized there was sort of no plot. On his ceiling was an electrical outlet, and when he plugged his phone into it, the phone dangled there in the air, pretty far down, turning slowly on its cord. I watched it instead of the movie.

He had a therapy appointment that afternoon — he'd have to drop me off after breakfast. We ate big breakfasts, and in traffic on the bridge he called his therapist to say he'd be running late; his therapist, he told me, really liked him, and wouldn't mind. By the time we arrived, the appointment time had already passed, so he called back and — since it was all the way across town — apologized, and cancelled. We went back to his place and watched television instead. At some point he told me about Mount St. Helens — how a man had caught the eruption in a photograph and sold it to the newspapers for a fortune — and I was amazed, so we went to the computer and he showed me the pictures. He told me the story of his ex-girlfriend as we walked. They'd been homeless together for a while, and it had made them very close; now that he had a place to live, she treated him like shit — never letting him talk to other girls, breaking up with him to go out with other boys, then calling to say mean things. He'd been meaning to break up with her, he said. They kept getting back together. We set out for a strip club across the bridge, but he got too tired, so we turned around. The walk back was quiet, and he played Venus in Furs on his iPhone — that thin little speaker our only company — and we both knew the words, so we sang along. Later a friend texted him about a night club. The club floor was white with lights underneath it, like that game with the polar bears — "don't break the ice" — and girls danced on poles, climbing down every once in a while to mingle with the crowd. A guy came up to chat me up — he was Palestinian, I think — and kept telling me I was too cute to bomb. I declined his offer of a drink. Trevor and I sat out on the curb while he smoked, watching a couple change clothes, or have sex, in a jeep across the street, while a man passed us leading a group of others and swinging a crowbar. Back inside, I danced on the little stage; when a guy on Molly tried to hug me, Trevor gave him a double high five. And then, when we finally got back to his place and into bed, his ex-girlfriend called. Something she said made it clear — she had been the threatening call before our date, her voice run through some kind of editing software, disguised. Now she was laughing at him, saying my date had probably gone badly. He said he was still on it. She got extremely pissed, told him never to call her again, and called back ten times. He didn't answer. He cried a little. I had a job interview at eleven the next morning, and instead I lay awake in the dark, his anxiety coming off him like heat, becoming mine — a kind I hadn't felt in a while. It bothered me that he could be so obsessed with this other girl while we were lying in the same bed. I cuddled him at first. Then I stopped. In the morning he drove me to my interview and waited in the car, napping. We had a long kiss before I got out. We made rough plans to see each other again.

name: Gabriel
dek: A policy of not looking at anyone I find attractive.
pages: We exchanged about six sentences on OkCupid before he asked if I wanted to hang out. The plan: wear overalls and go to Hot Topic, to be ironic. But on the day of our date he announced he'd been "just kidding" about the overalls, and I didn't like that — he wasn't taking our arrangement seriously, no matter how ridiculous it had been. I told him to meet me at my house. He said that I could be a murderer, or a rapist, and that he'd rather meet in a public place. Not entirely unreasonable — in another mood I might have admired his disregard for gender norms — but I reconsidered whether I wanted to meet him at all, and cancelled our date right then and there. He seemed surprised. So I changed my mind. I went into my room to make sure I was wearing clothes that didn't scream "I don't care if you think I'm pretty": a white ruffly button-down I'd never once considered wearing, which I thought perfect for my current sentiments. I put on the roll-on deodorant, and, since I was going all out, combed my hair with my fingers, getting engrossed in how much I could change its state. Then, since I had to wait for his call, I fell backwards onto my bed and lay there half-dreaming about absolutely nothing — and missed his call by seven minutes. He didn't pick up when I called back, so I texted him pictures of food and animals and smileys blowing heart kisses, walked the three houses to our meeting spot, and settled down next to a yield sign to study the percentage of white flowers embedded in the grass. I hadn't been outside yet that day; the gentle sun mushed my shoulders forward, sweetly. When he finally called, he was a few streets away, coming from work painting houses. His boss had criticized his work and cited it as the reason for his less-than-ideal pay, to which he'd replied: "then it's great that you're paying me what you are." I suggested this might have been a less than strategic response. Then I asked if we could meet for only a very short time, so we wouldn't have to suffer through an entire date — and caught myself: this reluctance, this uneasiness, was exactly the quality I hated most in my dates. So I left it at an invitation to my little intersection of white-flowered grass, and told him to see me not as a date but as a friend to be funny with. He came into view riding his bike like a steed — sitting fully upright, since his hands were cradling the phone.

I told him I liked his pants, and that was the last I saw of him, as I have a policy of not looking at anyone I find attractive — a policy that had come into effect, for the first time, that day. "Are you smoking a cigarette?" I asked. I wouldn't have to ask, he pointed out, if I'd been looking at him — which was one hundred percent the case — and I fell down laughing on the grass, imagining having to explain the policy's reasoning to him. His pants were spattered with paint from his job, and he was disappointed, he said, that people always commented on them; they were just his work clothes, so he didn't think they were cool. What I ideally would have noticed was the gold chain underneath the rim of his t-shirt. I noted that I did not have x-ray vision. This elaborate reasoning escaped him. I told him I would start looking at him, and that I was weird, and after convincing myself that everything was the way it always was, I shifted my head in his direction for a second while he talked. I was very proud of myself. His ex-girlfriend, he told me, had decided to become a stripper because she wanted her life to be more "real" — he seemed to find this silly, so I was, of course, compelled to tell him that I was an "aspiring alcoholic" for a surprisingly similar reason. He said everyone in this park was on an OkCupid date, and pointed at a couple in front of us who weren't wearing much: that was the way to do it — we should have come in our bathing suits. He was mostly looking to make friends in Portland, he said, since all his childhood friends had become gangster drug-addicts. I said I had no friends either, having only recently moved. We decided on beers from a store, and while he went inside he told me to watch his bike — and then, that I should not walk off with it. I was surprised, and could think of no reason he would distrust me. I felt, suddenly, profoundly misunderstood. There was nothing I could do. He came back with a paper bag and we drifted to another park, first the ground, then a picnic table, where he told me he liked to dress up sometimes — as a goth, in white tracksuits, as a gangster — and I told him I didn't know many boys who liked to play dress-up. I told him what had happened with David, and went to show him a picture, and found that I had been unmatched.

I chugged the last third of my beer and stood up feeling unhealthily drunk — the air gone opaque, a darker, deeper blue — and assigned myself the task of being extra careful about what came out of my mouth. He didn't want to pay for my dinner, he said; then, trying to explain himself, that he didn't want to pay for his own dinner either. At Los Gorditos I ordered a chimichanga much too large to finish, and we ate mostly in silence. After the meal he announced that he'd eaten too much and felt sick — where others might have hidden this, he was straightforward, as though it should be my problem too. How could one ask for support so casually? I told him he could come sit on my couch for a moment to feel better. At home, I pulled every piece of clothing out of my closet and introduced him to them one by one; his favorite was a bright orange long sleeve with a hologram of a dinosaur. He asked what I'd be doing if he weren't there, and I said, honestly, that I'd probably be on OkCupid — so he made me go on it while he watched. I'd been messaging someone about reading poetry to each other; Gabriel said I should just write "let's have sex," so I did. The responses arrived over the next few hours — first that he lived in North Portland and wanted foreplay, then "Oh I get it. Oh haha like 'we do sex now,'" then a third, something about poetry again. He saw my drawings and paintings and said, strangely: "Oh, I could actually use you for something — I really need to learn how to paint and draw. You could teach me." It is and has been my dream to give art lessons to a willing pupil, so I feigned disinterest, then thought better of it and told him I was seriously interested. When it got late, he said if he was going to bike home he'd better go. Outside, in the dark, standing behind his bike, he was just a glowy outline of a person — white, not much height, but some sort of presence — looking so forlorn. I'd stayed on the porch, under the light, leaving him no opportunity to hug or kiss me goodnight, which is perhaps what I intended. I said he could sleep on the couch if he really didn't want to bike; he said he would feel degraded to sleep on the couch. "Do you still want to do art lessons soon?" I asked, and he said, "Oh yeah — can I just, like, start coming by if I'm in the neighborhood?" I asked if he was being sarcastic, since that seemed a strange thing to ask at the end of a first date. He biked off — then called twenty-five minutes later: he'd forgotten his backpack. He came back for it, and this time I gave him a hug goodnight.
